source_text: Illic igitur et scripturarum et expositionum adulteratio deputanda est, ubi doctrinae diversitas invenitur. Quibus fuit propositum aliter docendi, cos necessitas coegit aliter disponendi instrumenta doctrinae. Alias enim non potuissent aliter docere, nisi aliter haberent per quae docerent. Sicut illis non potuisset succedere corruptela doctrinae sine corruptela instrumentorum eius, ita et nobis integritas doctrinae non competisset sine integritate eorum per quae doctrina tractatur. Etenim quid contrarium nobis in nostris? quid de proprio intulimus, ut aliquid contrarium ei et in scripturis deprehensum detractione vel adiectione vel transmutatione remediaremus? Quod sumus, hoc sunt scripturae ab initio suo. Ex illis sumus, antequam aliter fuit, antequam a vobis interpolarentur. Cum autem omnis interpolatio posterior credenda sit, veniens utique ex causa aemulationis, quae neque prior neque domestica unquam est eius quod aemulatur, tam incredibile est sapienti cuique, ut nos adulterum stilum intulisse videamur scripturis, qui sumus a principio et primi, quam illos non intulisse, qui sunt et posteri et adversi. Alius manu scripturas, alius sensus expositione intervertit. Neque enim si Valentinus integro instrumento uti videtur, non callidiore ingenio quam Marcion manus intulit veritati. Marcion enim exerte et palam machaera, non stilo usus est, quoniam ad materiam su(??)m caedem scripturarum confecit: Valentinus autem pepercit, quoniam non ad materiam scripturas, sed materiam ad scripturas excogitavit, et tamen plus abstulit et plus adiecit, auferens proprietates singulorum quoque verborum et adiciens dispositiones non comparentium rerum.
thought_title: Corruption of doctrine and corruption of the instruments go together
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that heretics have no right to use the Scriptures, and here he explains that doctrinal corruption necessarily involves corruption of the scriptural texts themselves.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore there, where diversity of doctrine is found, the adulteration both of the Scriptures and of their expositions must be reckoned to be. For those whose purpose was to teach differently, necessity compelled them to arrange differently the instruments of doctrine. For otherwise they could not have taught differently, unless they had differently the things through which they taught. Just as for them the corruption of doctrine could not have succeeded without the corruption of its instruments, so also for us the integrity of doctrine would not have been fitting without the integrity of those things through which doctrine is handled. For what is contrary to us in our things? What have we brought in from our own, so that we might remedy something contrary to it and found in the Scriptures by removal or addition or change? What we are, this the Scriptures are from their beginning. From them we are, before anything was otherwise, before they were interpolated by you. But since every interpolation must be believed to be later, coming certainly from a cause of rivalry, which is never prior nor domestic to that which it rivals, it is as incredible to every wise person that we, who are from the beginning and first, should seem to have brought an adulterous pen into the Scriptures, as that they, who are both later and opposed, should not have brought it in. One person overturns the Scriptures by hand, another by sense in exposition. For neither if Valentinus seems to use the instrument intact, did he not lay hands on the truth with a more cunning talent than Marcion. For Marcion openly and publicly used a sword, not a pen, since he made a slaughter of the Scriptures for his matter. But Valentinus spared them, since he did not devise the Scriptures for his matter, but the matter for the Scriptures, and yet he took away more and added more, taking away the properties even of individual words and adding arrangements of things that do not exist.

choices.why: Keeps the legal/documentary metaphor Tertullian uses for the Scriptures as the documentary instruments through which doctrine is conveyed.
Preserves the metaphor of falsifying a document by writing, matching the legal language of the passage.
Keeps the technical sense of the subject-matter or content that Marcion and Valentinus each adapted the Scriptures to.
Uses the technical term for tampering with a text, which Tertullian uses throughout this section.
Captures the contrast between Marcion's open violence and Valentinus's subtle cleverness.

pass_b_english: Wherever you find diversity of doctrine, there you must locate the adulteration of both the Scriptures and their interpretations. Those who set out to teach differently were forced by necessity to arrange the instruments of doctrine differently. They could not have taught differently unless they had different instruments through which to teach. Just as the corruption of doctrine could not have succeeded for them without the corruption of its instruments, so the integrity of doctrine would not have been ours without the integrity of the instruments through which doctrine is handled.

For what is there in our own writings that is contrary to us? What have we introduced from our own resources, that we should need to remedy something contrary to us found in the Scriptures by removal or addition or alteration? What we are, the Scriptures are from their beginning. We are from them, before anything was different, before they were interpolated by you. But since every interpolation must be believed to be later, coming as it does from the cause of rivalry, which is never prior to or native to that which it rivals, it is as incredible to any wise person that we, who are from the beginning and first, should be thought to have introduced an adulterous pen to the Scriptures, as it is incredible that they did not introduce one, who are both later and opposed.

One person corrupts the Scriptures with his hand, another with his interpretation of their meaning. For even if Valentinus seems to use the document intact, he did not lay hands on the truth with less cunning talent than Marcion. Marcion used a sword openly and plainly, not a pen, since he carried out the slaughter of the Scriptures for his matter. Valentinus, however, spared them, since he did not devise the Scriptures for his matter, but his matter for the Scriptures, and yet he took away more and added more, removing the distinctive properties of each individual word and adding arrangements of things that do not exist.
notes: The source text contains 'su(??)m' which appears to be damaged; the gloss renders it as 'his matter' based on context, but the exact reading is uncertain.

problems.quote: removing the proper meanings of individual words
problems.why: proprietates here means distinctive properties/force of words, not 'meanings'; contrasted with arrangements of non-existent things.
problems.fix: removing the distinctive properties of each individual word
problems.ruling: Latin 'proprietates' = properties/qualities, not 'meanings'; translation misstates nuance of word alteration.

edits.old: removing the proper meanings of individual words
edits.new: removing the distinctive properties of each individual word

fixed: Changed 'proper meanings' to 'distinctive properties' for proprietates, which refers to the distinctive force/properties of words, not their meanings.

problems.quote: what in our Scriptures is contrary to us?
problems.source_quote: Etenim quid contrarium nobis in nostris?
problems.why: Latin asks what is contrary to us in our own matters, not specifically in the Scriptures; English inserts 'Scriptures', changing the sense.
problems.fix: what, in our own matters, is contrary to us?
problems.ruling: Latin 'in nostris' means 'in our own things/matters'; inserting 'Scriptures' changes the sense.

edits.old: For what in our Scriptures is contrary to us?
edits.new: For what, in our own matters, is contrary to us?

fixed: Changed 'what in our Scriptures is contrary to us?' to 'what, in our own matters, is contrary to us?' because the Latin 'quid contrarium nobis in nostris?' refers to 'our things' generally, not specifically to the Scriptures.

polish.changed: Clarified the rhetorical questions by specifying 'our own writings' as the subject, smoothed sentence order, and made the contrast between Marcion and Valentinus flow more naturally for reading aloud while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.quote: For what, in our own matters, is contrary to us? What have we introduced from our own resources, that we should need to remedy something contrary to us found in the Scriptures by removal or addition or alteration?
notes.why: Rhetorical questions are tangled; 'what is contrary to us in our own matters' is circular and unclear.
notes.fix: Rewrite: 'What in our teaching contradicts itself? What have we added on our own that would require us to alter Scripture?'
